results.corrected_extracted: Post-marketing surveillance by an independent steering committee that the drug's sponsor, Ortho-McNeil Pharmaceuticals, set up on the recommendation of the FDA's Drug Abuse Advisory Committee when tramadol (Ultram) was marketed in the USA without scheduling. Reports came from spontaneous adverse-event reports to the company and the FDA (MedWatch: patients, pharmacists, physicians) and from a network of 110 NIDA-funded researchers and 145 other experts on drug use with access to about 250,000 people at risk for drug misuse, offered $75 for each completed questionnaire (average response 48.7% over 20 quarters); a subcommittee classified every report with DSM-IV-based ratings. No group of people who stopped tramadol without withdrawal, or who stopped another opioid, was studied (editors' reading of the design).
results.note: Numbers confirmed on the page (110, 145, 250,000, $75, 48.7%, 20 quarters). The paper calls Ortho-McNeil the sponsor of Ultram, never its manufacturer (p. 234); 'without scheduling' is on p. 233.

results.corrected_extracted: Withdrawal ratings (21 typical, 22 atypical) were used only when there was no drug-seeking or other evidence of 'abuse'; reports with withdrawal and drug-seeking were rated as 'abuse'. Because unusual symptoms appeared as the study progressed, all withdrawal cases of 1995–2000 were rescored as typical or atypical. Typical withdrawal needed at least three DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms; atypical withdrawal also had a strong component of other CNS disturbances, and is described as always accompanied by typical symptoms (3.1), as often combined with them (Table 2, footnote b) and, in the Discussion (p. 238), as occurring in addition to or in place of them. The authors say 'atypical' is a descriptor, not a claim that there are two syndromes. No check of agreement between raters is reported.
results.corrected_locator: 2.2 Detailed methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 235, the 5th continuing p. 236); Table 1 (p. 235); Table 2, footnotes a and b, and 3.1, 1st paragraph (p. 236); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 238)
results.note: Text confirmed unchanged; only page and locator completed, because the 'in addition to or in place of' wording sits in the Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 238), which the locator omitted.

results.corrected_extracted: The abstract says withdrawal of either type made up nearly 40% of all adverse events reported, and the Discussion calls it the most prevalent adverse event (nearly 40% of total cases); Table 3 gives 33%, and 644 of the same 1,248 reports were rated as 'abuse' (3.2, p. 237).
results.corrected_locator: Abstract (p. 233); Table 3 and 3.2, 1st paragraph (p. 237); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 238)
results.note: Text confirmed unchanged; locator completed with Table 3 and 3.2 (p. 237), which the text cites. The paper does not say outright that the 644 are among the 1,248, but adds them within 'this study'.

results.corrected_extracted: Typical withdrawal symptoms listed: abdominal cramps, anxiety, bone pain, depression, diarrhoea, goose flesh, insomnia, tearing, nausea, restlessness, runny nose and sweating (no frequencies). Among the 55 atypical cases: severe anxiety and panic attacks 32.8%; unusual CNS symptoms (confusion, delusions, depersonalization, derealization, paranoia) 27.2%; unusual sensory phenomena (numbness, tingling, paresthesia, tinnitus) 25.4%; hallucinations (tactile, visual, auditory) 20.0%; the total exceeds 100% because several were reported together. Editors' calculation: the nearest counts of 55 (18, 15, 14 and 11) give 32.7%, 27.3%, 25.5% and 20.0% when rounded, or 32.7%, 27.2%, 25.4% and 20.0% when cut off; no single rule gives all four printed percentages, so they cannot all come from 55.
results.note: Table 2 values confirmed on the page. Recomputed: cut off instead of rounded, 15/55 and 14/55 give the printed 27.2% and 25.4%; only 32.8% fits neither way, so 'three cannot come from 55' overstated it.
3.2: 644 abuse-rated reports, withdrawal symptoms in 121 (typical) and 3 (atypical); 'at least 546' is the authors' figure. Recomputed 422 + 124 = 546; 546/1248 = 43.75%, 43.8%.

results.corrected_extracted: Age was known for only 139 of 455 withdrawal cases (a total that matches neither 422 nor 546), with no figures given; sex was known in 82% of typical and 87% of atypical cases, of whom about 56% were women (55.8% and 56.3%); the authors say this suggests both types may be more common in women, but that the data do not appear to establish any relation between sex and withdrawal.
results.note: All numbers confirmed (3.3, p. 237). The authors first say the data suggest both types may be more common in women, then that the data 'do not appear to establish' a relation; suggestion and hedge restored.

results.corrected_extracted: Length of exposure was known in about 50% of withdrawal cases: many followed brief exposures of 3–4 days, with no clustering after long exposure (no counts). Maintenance dose was known in 63% of typical cases (50–2,000 mg a day; 92% at or below the maximum recommended level of 400 mg a day) and 78% of atypical cases (50–1,300 mg a day); the paper gives 25% of all atypical cases as above 400 mg, three times the 8% of typical cases, without saying whether the base is all atypical cases or those with a known dose (no counts or test). Atypical cases tended to last longer and to be harder to manage.
results.note: All figures confirmed (pp. 237–238). The paper says 25% 'of all atypical cases', so the base is left open instead of being placed inside the 78% with a known dose.

results.corrected_extracted: Withdrawal followed abrupt discontinuation, which the authors say many physicians did despite the label's warning, and in some instances dose reductions or a tapered stop. Most physicians described relatively mild cases that they monitored without treatment and that usually resolved in 2 or 3 days; as severity increased, treatment was often necessary. The committee's clinicians drew on about 75 consultations; no counts are given, and outcomes only in general terms.
results.note: 3.5 says treatment was 'often necessary' as severity increased (hedge restored). Outcomes are given in general words (resolved in 2–3 days; most atypical symptoms responded), so 'no outcomes' was too strong; treatment details deliberately not added.
2.3 exposure algorithm and all rate statements confirmed. Figure 1 at 300 dpi: typical counts sum to 367, atypical to 55; May 1996 quarter 37 and 10, total plotted about 2.27; last quarter about 0.3.
Discussion, 8th paragraph (pp. 239–240): FDA estimate of about 10% (Kessler, 1993); after several years 'probably' considerably less than 5%, as stated.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors say the atypical symptoms were more like those reported on stopping SSRI antidepressants than on stopping opioids, may relate to tramadol's reported noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibition, which remains to be determined, and could be misdiagnosed as psychosis or delirium. They report no difference between typical and atypical cases in age, sex, length of exposure or history of drug misuse (figures shown only for sex), so they could define no feature that would indicate who may be at risk of atypical symptoms, with one possible exception: more atypical cases had been at doses above 400 mg a day (25% against 8%).
results.note: The paper says 'with one possible exception' (hedge restored). Age and length of exposure, like history, have no typical-versus-atypical figures (3.3, 3.4), so 'the last without data shown' became 'figures shown only for sex'.

results.corrected_extracted: 1006 Finnish autopsy cases toxicologically investigated at the Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, in 1995–2000, whose cause of death a forensic pathologist had established as poisoning by alcohol, a single drug or both (where both, the more important cause cited first on the death certificate). Femoral blood taken at autopsy into 1% sodium fluoride and kept at 4 °C; alcohol measured in every sample and a broad drug screen in about 83% of cases, at the pathologist's request; blood alcohol given in parts per thousand, mass per mass. The nine drugs were those present in at least 20 fatal poisonings of each type; limit of quantitation 0.02 mg/L for temazepam. Each drug's lowest included concentration was the bottom of its therapeutic range, except temazepam, counted from 0.1 mg/L because effects can occur below the therapeutic level; mixed poisonings needed blood alcohol of at least 0.50. Caffeine, nicotine and small amounts of 2-propanol and acetone were allowed in the cases; the 615 deaths from alcohol alone were free of other analytes in the screens; low concentrations (under 1 mg/L) of diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, nordazepam or demoxepam were allowed in the mixed groups.
results.note: All details confirmed (Methods, 1st–4th paragraphs, p. 282). The paper allows caffeine, nicotine and small amounts of 2-propanol and acetone just before saying pure alcohol poisonings were free of other analytes, so 'every other substance' was too absolute.

Table 3 at 300 dpi: 3.3 (2.8, 3.8; 1.0–6.2) and 2.5 (2.0, 3.0; 0.7–4.3), 0.8 (24), P<0.001; Figure 1 temazepam whiskers at −1.0 and −0.6; text ranges against Table 3 and median differences recomputed.

results.corrected_extracted: Temazepam group split at 0.7 mg/L (the divide counted in the low half): 28 deaths at or below, median blood alcohol 2.9; 29 above, median 2.1; printed point estimate of the difference 0.9 (the printed medians differ by 0.8), P < 0.001. With the 18 deaths in which temazepam was only below its therapeutic range (under 0.4 mg/L) set aside, the median blood alcohol in the remaining 39 was 2.2 (95% CI 2.1–2.5). The authors read the higher-concentration halves' lower medians as suggesting a positive concentration–effect relationship.
results.note: Table 4 and Results text confirmed (0.7; 28 and 29; 2.9 and 2.1; 0.9; P<0.001; 18 below 0.4 mg/L; 39 cases, 2.2, 2.1–2.5). The authors write 'suggesting' a concentration–effect relationship; hedge restored.

Table 1 checked on the page: all counts and percentages as stated; 33/57 = 57.9% against the printed 46; 24/57 = 42%. Results 1st paragraph: 53 years and 88% against 46 and 70%; Methods 8th paragraph: pairwise tests only.
Table 2 on the page: temazepam 18, 13, 26 (46); median 0.8; range 0.4–0.9; benzodiazepine-positive 30%; 24–47% across groups. Results 3rd paragraph asserts no effect on the medians with no numbers.

results.corrected_extracted: Temazepam is the only benzodiazepine among the nine drugs studied, which were those present in at least 20 fatal poisonings of each type. The authors cite their own earlier paper (reference 20: Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2002;26:956–959; not read here) as finding that temazepam lowered the blood alcohol at which a given share of alcohol poisonings occurs, while with diazepam, chlordiazepoxide or desmethyldiazepam at concentrations up to 1 mg/L the blood alcohol did not differ from pure alcohol poisonings, and say that in that study diazepam and chlordiazepoxide appeared significantly safer than temazepam with alcohol.
results.note: Introduction, 5th paragraph, and reference 20 confirmed. The Discussion says diazepam and chlordiazepoxide 'appeared to be significantly safer'; 'as showing' had dropped that hedge.

results.corrected_extracted: Printed differences in median blood alcohol from the alcohol-only deaths: citalopram 0.3 (P > 0.05), diltiazem 0.6 (P = 0.006), zopiclone 0.6, temazepam 0.8, levomepromazine 0.9, amitriptyline 1.5, propoxyphene 1.6, doxepin 1.6, promazine 1.9 (each P < 0.001). Fatal toxicity index (annual deaths divided by annual sales in defined daily doses per 1000 inhabitants per day): temazepam 0.9 (95% CI 0.7–1.1; 14.33 deaths and 15.95 sold a year) and zopiclone 0.9 (0.7–1.2), the lowest of the nine; promazine 120.8 (97.7–143.9), the highest. Temazepam's 14.33 deaths a year come to about 86 over the six years (editors' calculation), more than the 57 deaths with alcohol, so the index is not limited to deaths with alcohol. The authors say this division reflects not only acute toxicity but also how the drugs are used, some taken deliberately in overdose for intoxication or with suicidal intent, and that more information is needed to separate behaviour from the drugs' own toxicity.
results.note: All Table 3 and Table 5 figures confirmed; 14.33 × 6 = 86. The paper says some are deliberately taken in overdoses for intoxication purposes or with suicidal intent; the intoxication motive is restored.

Discussion, 1st paragraph (pp. 283–284): pharmacodynamic effects more important, mechanisms not fully elucidated; combined effect generally considered additive and usually non-pharmacokinetic; stated without data or citation.

Acknowledgements (p. 31): Solvay Duphar Award lecture by R.R.G.; NIDA grants RO1 DA03889 and DA01147. No search method anywhere. Text says 26 papers (p. 7); tables hold 13 and 17, Roache et al. 1997 in press. Motive passage p. 6.

results.corrected_extracted: Table 2: 13 studies in people with 'histories of drug abuse', 2 to 16 people each, men in all but one (Healey and Pickens 1983: men and women, n = 10); drug given orally and double-blind except two early studies; 11 of the 13 have the review's first author as co-author (editors' count from the reference list); four (Griffiths et al. 1976, Bigelow et al. 1976, Healey and Pickens 1983, Troisi et al. 1993) had no placebo comparison (editors' count). The text says comparisons within and across the studies suggest that the person's history is the most important single determinant, and that these studies almost invariably showed reinforcement: diazepam chosen over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% by 16 men; triazolam a reinforcer in 4 of 6 men and, in another study of 8 men, only before a relaxation task; lorazepam was chosen over buspirone by 7 of 8, but with no placebo the table calls it unclear whether lorazepam was a reinforcer. Doses (study conditions) were mostly far above those in Table 3 (editors' comparison), for example diazepam 50–400 mg, 40–160 mg and 40 or 80 mg in three studies; the text says higher doses were usually associated with greater reinforcing effects than lower doses.
results.note: All counts confirmed on the 200-dpi tables and the reference list. Restored the review's 'suggest' and Table 2's caveat that lorazepam's reinforcement is unclear without placebo; marked the dose comparison as the editors'.

Table 3 at 200 dpi: 28, 27 and 76% (n=10); 16% and 20% (12 each); 25, 32 and 38% (12, 13, 11); 28% estimated; 33% (43); 38 and 48% (13, 14). 12 of 17 with de Wit or Johanson (reference list); text p. 13.

results.corrected_extracted: Moderate social drinkers chose diazepam over placebo in three studies: 100% of choices (12 people), 73% (14) and 64% (30; buspirone 27% in 25 others); light drinkers tested in two of them (means of 12 and 4 drinks a week for the moderate and light drinkers of those two studies) chose it on 66% (a non-significant tendency, 18 people) and 40% (13), the light–moderate difference significant in the second. In both studies with light drinkers the moderate drinkers had significantly more weekly marijuana use (26% on average across the three studies), and a pooled analysis found that people who chose diazepam reported more current marijuana and lifetime stimulant use; the review says this was not investigated prospectively. Elsewhere it says that people with histories of moderate drinking and men with alcoholism showed increased sensitivity to the reinforcing and positive mood effects of benzodiazepines (no figures), and it calls the implications of moderate drinkers' preference for later risk unclear.
results.note: Figures confirmed (Table 3; pp. 5, 13–14, 30–31). The 12 and 4 drinks a week are given only for the two de Wit studies, not Evans. Figure 2 plots another measure, the share preferring diazepam (100%, about 71%, about 70%).

results.corrected_extracted: Anxious people, five double-blind studies, mixed: in the two with a single morning dose and a return to daily activities diazepam was not a reinforcer and placebo was preferred (Table 3 marks diazepam as a punisher in both; de Wit et al. 1986; McCracken et al. 1990, 14 people seeking treatment, 10 mg diazepam on 37% of sessions); the three giving control over time and total amount found preference: 65% of evening choice sessions in 22 anxious people against 45% in 23 controls (marginal, P = 0.06), with more capsules taken; 3 of 4 women with generalized anxiety disorder chose diazepam exclusively, and 11 of 14 people with generalized anxiety or panic disorder showed clear alprazolam preference, taking capsules 'as needed' for 4 weeks, most at low, stable rates. Insomnia: triazolam chosen on 86% of nights under a forced choice with placebo (three groups of 8, one per condition), but capsules taken on 77% and 80% of nights when only triazolam or only placebo was on offer, and in other studies placebo taken on more than 60% of nights, not different from triazolam. The review says a comparison of Table 3 studies, not investigated prospectively, suggests that benzodiazepines are more likely to function as reinforcers, or less likely as punishers, when people control the time and total amount.
results.note: All figures confirmed (Table 3 at 200 dpi; pp. 14–15). 'No preference' understated the single-dose studies (placebo preferred); the text says placebo use was 'not different from' triazolam; the cross-study comparison 'suggests'.
p. 5 as stated: 7.1% cited to NIDA Press Office (1995), an HHS News release of 15 December 1995; about half cited to Johnston et al. (1993), survey results 1975–1992.

key_findings.correction: Reports came from two sources: spontaneous reports received by the drug's sponsor, Ortho-McNeil, from patients, pharmacists, physicians and the FDA (MedWatch), and a key-informant network of 110 NIDA grantees and 145 other experts with access to about 250,000 people at risk for misuse, offered $75 per completed questionnaire; the average informant response rate over the 20 quarters was 48.7%.

Age was known for only 139 of 455 withdrawal cases (no figures given; the authors say the ages appear to indicate that age is not an important predisposing factor). Sex was known in 82% of typical and 87% of atypical cases; about 56% were women (55.8% and 56.3%).

Length of exposure was known in about 50% of withdrawal cases and was a weak factor: many cases followed relatively brief exposures of 3–4 days, with no clustering after long exposure (no counts). Maintenance dose was known in 63% of typical cases (range 50–2000 mg per day; 92% at or below 400 mg per day) and 78% of atypical cases (range 50–1300 mg per day); the paper gives 25% of all atypical cases as above 400 mg per day, about three times the 8% of typical cases, without saying whether the base is all atypical cases or those with a known dose. Atypical cases tended to last longer and to be harder to manage.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The abstract (p. 233) and Discussion (p. 238) say withdrawal made up nearly 40% of all adverse events; Table 3 gives 422 of 1248, printed as 33% (editors' arithmetic: 33.8%). | consequence: The 'nearly 40%' matches neither count (33.8% of reports rated withdrawal; 43.8% if the 124 abuse-rated reports with withdrawal symptoms are added), so it is not simply an overstatement; a claim should use one of these with its basis stated.

issue: The text says both kinds of withdrawal may be more common in women, then that the data do not appear to establish any relation with sex (p. 237); no figures for the sex of people prescribed tramadol are given. | consequence: The 56% of women among reported cases cannot be read as a higher risk in women.

risk_of_bias.note: Design (case series), JBI-prevalence domains and overall high agreed. METHODS §5.3 lists no instrument for case series; the JBI domains follow existing case-series cards and each judgment fits the paper.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. results_show should not say 'per quarter ... in the first year': the paper gives no time unit (the card's own RI1) and the peak came 12–15 months after launch. The management advice has outcomes in general words, not none.

missed: The Discussion says withdrawal could serve as a factor leading to abuse (p. 238) and then that withdrawal without drug-seeking has little or no relationship to abuse (p. 239); the card cites only the second.

The Discussion calls withdrawal a prominent and common feature of a large number of people rated positive for abuse (p. 238); 3.2 gives 124 of 644 positive, possible or alleged abuse reports (19%, editors' calculation; p. 237).
The Ultram label of the time warned of typical but not atypical withdrawal (Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 238).
design_detail and funding.affiliations_note call Ortho-McNeil 'the manufacturer'; the paper calls it the sponsor of Ultram (p. 234).
analysis.effect_sizes gives the 25% above 400 mg as a share of atypical cases with dose data; the paper says 25% of all atypical cases (p. 238).

key_findings.correction: The printed differences from the alcohol-only median (Table 3) were 1.5–1.9 for amitriptyline (median BAC 1.6, difference 1.5), propoxyphene (1.7, 1.6), doxepin (1.6, 1.6) and promazine (1.3, 1.9), and 0.6–0.9 for zopiclone (2.7, 0.6), diltiazem (2.8, 0.6), temazepam (2.5, 0.8) and levomepromazine (2.6, 0.9); the Results text gives 1.6–2.0 and 0.6–0.7 for these groups (p. 283; diltiazem not named). Citalopram (3.1, difference 0.3) was the only group without a significant difference (P>0.05); all others had P<0.001 except diltiazem (P=0.006). Note: the printed point estimates are probably Hodges–Lehmann estimates from the Mann–Whitney procedure, which the paper does not state; for amitriptyline and doxepin they differ from 3.3 minus the group median (1.7) by 0.2 and 0.1. [The card's 1.6–2.0 came from the text, not Table 3, where amitriptyline is 1.5.]

Fatal toxicity index (annual deaths divided by annual sales in defined daily doses per 1000 inhabitants per day), 1995-2000: promazine 120.8 (95% CI 97.7-143.9), levomepromazine 47.3 (37.0-57.7), propoxyphene 32.0 (23.3-40.7), doxepin 20.9 (15.0-26.8), amitriptyline 12.2 (9.3-15.2), citalopram 1.4 (1.1-1.7), diltiazem 1.4 (1.1-1.7), zopiclone 0.9 (0.7-1.2), temazepam 0.9 (0.7-1.1). Note: The denominator is sales, not the number of people taking the drug or the number of prescriptions; the index mixes a drug's toxicity with who takes it and how. The two hypnotics of the nine, temazepam and zopiclone, have the lowest indices. [Finding confirmed; 'the two sedatives' was wrong, since levomepromazine and promazine, with the highest indices, are also used for sedation.]
page: pp. 284, 286; locator: Table 3, promazine row, Maximum column (p. 284); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 286)

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Table 1 prints the doxepin group's mean age as 45 with a range of 26-40, so the mean lies outside its own range. | consequence: At least one figure in that row is wrong (probably the upper bound of the range). Ages from Table 1 should not be cited without flagging this; checked on the rendered page, so it is not an extraction error. [Propoxyphene part dropped: a mean of 43 in a range of 28-47 is unusual but possible, and the share of suicides says nothing about age.]

issue: The printed point estimates of the difference in median BAC do not equal the difference of the printed medians in six groups: printed smaller for amitriptyline (3.3 minus 1.6 = 1.7, printed 1.5), doxepin (1.7, printed 1.6) and promazine (2.0, printed 1.9); printed larger for citalopram (0.2, printed 0.3), diltiazem (0.5, printed 0.6) and levomepromazine (0.7, printed 0.9). | consequence: The printed values are evidently Hodges-Lehmann estimates from the Mann-Whitney test rather than differences of medians, but the paper does not say so; a reader subtracting the medians will get different numbers. Both should be reported together if cited.

issue: Eighteen significance tests are reported (nine comparisons with the alcohol-only deaths, Table 3, and nine high-against-low subgroup comparisons, Table 4), and nine FTIs are given with confidence intervals (Table 5), without any correction for multiplicity; twelve P values are printed only as inequalities (P>0.05 twice and P>0.5 for the non-significant ones, P<0.001 nine times). | consequence: The borderline results (diltiazem P=0.006; promazine subgroup P=0.025) are less secure than they look, and exact P values are missing wherever an inequality is printed.

issue: In Table 1, accidental plus suicide leaves 1-11 cases per group unaccounted for (58 of the 391 mixed deaths), presumably of undetermined manner, while the cause-of-death columns sum exactly to each n. The Results text speaks of drug poisonings ruled accidental (57) or undetermined (140), but its 'undetermined' counts for levomepromazine, amitriptyline, propoxyphene and promazine (14, 20, 42 and 18) equal Table 1's suicide counts, and 140 is close to the 141 suicides. | consequence: The text appears to call suicides 'undetermined'; the deaths of undetermined manner in Table 1 are described nowhere, and the table's percentages do not add to 100.

issue: The study's one benzodiazepine, temazepam, was included with a lower concentration cut-off (0.1 mg/L) than its therapeutic range would give (0.4 mg/L), on the stated reasoning that effects can occur below the therapeutic level, while every other drug was cut at the bottom of its therapeutic range. | consequence: The temazepam group therefore includes 18 cases that would have been excluded under the rule applied to the other eight drugs, which lowers the group's median drug concentration; without them the median BAC falls from 2.5 to 2.2 (the authors' own sensitivity analysis), so including them raised the group's median BAC and made the difference from alcohol alone smaller. Both figures should be cited together.

risk_of_bias.note: Design, ROBINS-E and overall very high agreed. Two notes overstate: the promazine group is not 'explicitly' people prescribed it for withdrawal (the paper describes Finnish prescribing in general, p. 286), and Tables 3 and 4 hold 18 tests, not 19.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed, but: 53 against 46 years is about seven years, not 'a decade' (also in selection_effects); concentrations above the therapeutic range reach 81–96% in five groups, not six; that the high halves are largely intentional overdoses is an unshown inference.

missed: The Results text says the high- and low-concentration halves differed significantly (P<0.05) in every group, but Table 4 gives P>0.05 for zopiclone and P>0.5 for citalopram (pp. 283, 285); the abstract excludes only citalopram.

Table 5's annual deaths exceed the alcohol-drug groups (temazepam 14.33 a year, about 86 over 1995-2000, against 57 with alcohol), so the FTI counts deaths outside the 1006, presumably including deaths without alcohol; the paper does not say where they come from.

Not every FTI equals the printed annual deaths divided by annual sales (propoxyphene 46.83/1.43 = 32.7, printed 32.0; zopiclone 20.17/21.04 = 0.96, printed 0.9; editors' calculation), so how the FTIs and their intervals were computed is not fully described.
The Discussion cites Table 1 for the promazine maximum BAC equalling the alcohol-only median; those figures are in Table 3 (p. 286).
n_outcomes_tested (19) and the risk-of-bias note's 'Nineteen comparisons' do not match the 18 tests in Tables 3 and 4.

key_findings.correction: Non-medical use, as cited: 7.1% of the US high-school class of 1995 reported non-medical use of tranquilizers (mostly benzodiazepines; cited to a 1995 press release), and about half of people who used them reported usually getting high from them (cited to an earlier survey report, Johnston et al. 1993, so the two figures do not describe the same people); most non-medical use is oral and alongside other drugs, with high rates among people using heroin and people on methadone maintenance. [The card's 'about half of those' joined two different surveys, against its own RI6.]

Drug reinforcement is defined without regard to motive: taking a benzodiazepine to feel good, to avoid anxiety or to avoid withdrawal symptoms all count as reinforcement. The authors speculate that a more general reinforcement mechanism may explain much of long-term use better than therapeutic effect alone, since many long-term patients report trouble controlling use and taking it to avoid withdrawal, and long-term efficacy has not been clearly shown. [The paper calls this speculation and says 'may provide a more satisfactory explanation for much of' long-term use, not that it 'best explains most'.]

The authors judge the person's history to be the most important single determinant of whether a benzodiazepine works as a reinforcer. Studies in people with histories of drug abuse almost always found that it did (Table 2, 13 studies; for example diazepam chosen over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% in 16 men), with higher doses usually more reinforcing, benzodiazepines less reinforcing than pentobarbital and more than chlorpromazine, buspirone or abecarnil, and diazepam more than oxazepam. Lorazepam was chosen over buspirone by 7 of 8, but with no placebo the table calls it unclear whether lorazepam was a reinforcer; four of the 13 studies had no placebo comparison (editors' count).

Moderate social drinkers chose diazepam over placebo in three studies, light drinkers did not (in the two de Wit studies, means of 12 and 4 drinks a week): diazepam choice 100% against 66% (de Wit et al. 1989; 12 and 18 people), 73% against 40% (de Wit & Doty 1994; 14 and 13 people; the difference was significant), and 64% in the 30 moderate drinkers tested with diazepam, against 27% choice of buspirone in the 25 tested with it (Evans et al. 1996). The percentage of moderate drinkers who preferred diazepam (2 or 3 of 3 choices) was 100%, about 71% and about 70%. About 30% of 20- to 40-year-olds meet or exceed the criteria for moderate drinking. [The drinking means are given for the two de Wit studies only, p. 13.]

The authors suggest, noting that it was not investigated prospectively, that occasional recreational drug use not meeting criteria for abuse or dependence may be associated with choosing diazepam: in both studies contrasting moderate with light drinkers, the moderate drinkers used marijuana weekly significantly more often (weekly use averaged 26% among moderate drinkers in the three studies), and in a pooled analysis of earlier diazepam choice studies in volunteers screened to exclude substance abuse or dependence, people who chose diazepam reported more current marijuana use and more lifetime stimulant use (Chutuape & de Wit 1994).

In anxious people, five double-blind studies gave mixed results. In the two using a single morning dose diazepam was not a reinforcer and placebo was preferred (Table 3 marks diazepam as a punisher in both; de Wit et al. 1986; McCracken et al. 1990: 14 people seeking treatment chose 10 mg diazepam on 37% of sessions). Three that let people control timing and total amount found preference: 22 anxious volunteers chose diazepam on 65% of evening sessions against 45% for 23 controls (marginal, P=0.06) and took more capsules (Chutuape & de Wit 1995); 3 of 4 women with generalized anxiety disorder chose diazepam exclusively, and 11 of 14 people with generalized anxiety or panic disorder showed clear alprazolam preference, mostly at low, stable rates, when taking capsules as needed for 4 weeks (Roache et al. 1996, 1997).

In people with insomnia, triazolam was chosen on 86% of nights when a mutually exclusive choice with placebo was offered (three groups of 8; Roehrs et al. 1997); under optional self-administration, placebo was taken on more than 60% of nights, not different from triazolam (capsules taken on 77% of nights in the triazolam condition and 80% in the placebo condition) (Roehrs et al. 1992, 1996, 1997).

risk_of_bias.note: Narrative review, editors' checklist and overall high agreed; domain notes match the paper (no search, footnoted exclusions, 11 of 13 Table 2 studies co-authored by the first author). RI5 checked against de Wit et al. 1986 (pp. 536, 540): confirmed.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial, not minor: the central claim that drug history is the most important determinant rests on cross-study comparisons in which drug-experienced people got far higher doses, which the review never discusses, and the abstract states reinforcement in anxiety and insomnia without the body's mixed results.

missed: Four of the 13 Table 2 studies had no placebo comparison (Griffiths et al. 1976, Bigelow et al. 1976, Healey and Pickens 1983, Troisi et al. 1993; editors' count), and the text names alprazolam, diazepam, oxazepam and triazolam, not lorazepam, as shown reinforcers (pp. 7–9).

For de Wit & Doty (1994), Table 3's results column says moderate drinkers only tended to prefer diazepam (73%); its reinforcer label rests on the reviewers' one-tailed tests (footnotes c and d, pp. 11, 13).
